messages.author: 5db21e7785ef2433
messages.subject: Size of the reserve considered
parts:
Hi all,

I am currently working on the pcount model. But one of my major concern, is how the size of the reserve is considered in the codes? I am working in a fenced game reserve, so can the model estimate the size of the population without knowing the size of the reserve?

Thank you for answers.

Anne

messages.author: ee269fd5c4d17761
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Size of the reserve considered
parts:
The model gives estimates of abundance (or density) per sample unit. The definition of sample unit isn't always clear. If your samples came from a defined sample area (e.g. 20 m radius), then you can extrapolate from the sample area to the study area. If your sample area is undefined (e.g. you recorded every animal you could detect, but it's unclear how large an area that is), then it's harder to get a precise estimate of the population size over the whole reserve. You could guess what your sample area is (probably make 3 guesses: the minimum, best guess, and maximum areas you think realistic) and make extrapolations based on each of them. Also keep in mind that if you have habitat covariates on the abundance estimates that you'll need to account for those habitat covariates across the entire reserve. (If you have a map of covariate values across the reserve, you could create a grid with boxes equal in size to your estimated sample area. Then estimate the abundance in each of those grid cells and add them together.)

Philip Shirk
Postdoctoral Scholar
Cooperative Institute of Marine Resources Studies
Oregon State University

messages.author: 02d195331194f5bd
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Size of the reserve considered
parts:
Start by converting the estimated density from individuals per sample plots to individuals per hectare. Then, ignoring the habitat covariate, that would also be your estimate of density for the whole reserve. You could multiply the density by the reserve area to get the total number of individuals in the reserve. But with the habitat covariate, you want to split up the reserve into a bunch of little boxes that each the same size as your sample areas. So if your reserve is 100 ha and each sample area is 1 ha, you would have 100 boxes. Get the average tree cover in each of those boxes and use the fit model to predict the density in each of the 100 boxes. (All boxes that have the same habitat will have the same predicted density.) Once you have those, you can just add together the number of organisms in all the boxes to get the total number in the reserve. The transect replicates that you have are necessary for fitting the original model, but not for extrapolating the results. 

Philip Shirk

Le 15 févr. 2021 à 21:22, Philip Shirk <philip...@gmail.com> a écrit :

The model gives estimates of abundance (or density) per sample unit. The definition of sample unit isn't always clear. If your samples came from a defined sample area (e.g. 20 m radius), then you can extrapolate from the sample area to the study area. If your sample area is undefined (e.g. you recorded every animal you could detect, but it's unclear how large an area that is), then it's harder to get a precise estimate of the population size over the whole reserve. You could guess what your sample area is (probably make 3 guesses: the minimum, best guess, and maximum areas you think realistic) and make extrapolations based on each of them. Also keep in mind that if you have habitat covariates on the abundance estimates that you'll need to account for those habitat covariates across the entire reserve. (If you have a map of covariate values across the reserve, you could create a grid with boxes equal in size to your estimated sample area. Then estimate the abundance in each of those grid cells and add them together.)

Philip Shirk
Postdoctoral Scholar
Cooperative Institute of Marine Resources Studies
Oregon State University

Le 17 févr. 2021 à 07:11, Philip Shirk <fil...@gmail.com> a écrit :

Start by converting the estimated density from individuals per sample plots to individuals per hectare. Then, ignoring the habitat covariate, that would also be your estimate of density for the whole reserve. You could multiply the density by the reserve area to get the total number of individuals in the reserve. But with the habitat covariate, you want to split up the reserve into a bunch of little boxes that each the same size as your sample areas. So if your reserve is 100 ha and each sample area is 1 ha, you would have 100 boxes. Get the average tree cover in each of those boxes and use the fit model to predict the density in each of the 100 boxes. (All boxes that have the same habitat will have the same predicted density.) Once you have those, you can just add together the number of organisms in all the boxes to get the total number in the reserve. The transect replicates that you have are necessary for fitting the original model, but not for extrapolating the results. 

Philip Shirk
